reason: The amino acids and phospholipids are shown supplying protein and membrane growth, matching the first goal.
expectation: The cell will grow by making proteins and expanding its membranes.

effect: The cell has grown, but its DNA remains uncopied, so copying is the next step toward the goal.
reaction: The time arrow makes the distinction between growth and DNA copying clear.
reason: DNA nucleotides are the building blocks needed to copy the cell's DNA.
expectation: The cell will copy its DNA in preparation for division.

effect: The DNA is copied, and the new goal is to separate the copies and divide the cell.
reaction: The distinct line styles help distinguish old and newly synthesized DNA.
reason: The spindle cutaway shows microtubules attaching to duplicated chromosomes and extending toward opposite poles, matching the separation goal.
expectation: The spindle will separate the chromosome copies toward opposite poles.

effect: The chromosome copies have separated into two nuclei, but the cell still shares one cytoplasm and outer membrane.
reaction: The intermediate inset clarifies how the copies moved apart.
reason: The actin–myosin ring is positioned at the cell's equator, where it can divide the shared cell.
expectation: The ring will constrict and split the cell into two daughters.

effect: The ring completed division into two daughter cells, and the repeated pairs show how further divisions can build a population. Both chapter goals are complete.
reaction: The tightening sequence makes the final physical separation easy to follow.

mostWorthwhile.text: Separating the chromosome copies before dividing the cytoplasm was worthwhile: the two stages made clear why two nuclei are present before the cell splits.

leastWorthwhile.text: The growth step was fairly predictable, though its planned time arrow usefully separated growth from DNA copying.

surprise.text: The final picture extended one division into a population, including cells retained for further division.

arbitrary.text: No action felt purposeless; the pictures and goals suggested the sequence. The term “centrosomes” was not explained, though the spindle picture showed their position and microtubules.

continue.text: I would continue to see how the daughter cells take different paths, although this chapter's combinations were mostly straightforward.
